subject: Mathematics
source: National Curriculum (KS2 Year 6: number and place value to 10,000,000, negative numbers, written methods for the four operations, order of operations, common factors, multiples and primes); Drive Maths folder checked (national curriculum documents only for KS2), lessons written from the National Curriculum

lessons.title: Reading and writing numbers to 10,000,000
objectives: Read and write numbers up to 10,000,000 in numerals and words
Give the value of each digit in a 7- or 8-digit number

keywords.def: 1,000,000; one thousand thousands
10,000,000; ten millions
one of the symbols 0 to 9
the value a digit has because of its position

starter: Say Bismillah. Write four hundred and six thousand and nine as a number.
What is the value of the 8 in 482,150?

teach.heading: Three groups of three
bullets: 7,284,509 has a 7 in the millions place.
Commas split the number into groups of three.
teach.note: Use a place value chart with M, HTh, TTh, Th, H, T, O. Remind pupils that every group of three digits is read like a 3-digit number followed by the group name.

teach.heading: Reading 7,284,509
bullets: 509. Seven million, two hundred and eighty-four thousand, five hundred and nine.
teach.note: Say each group aloud. Pupils often skip the word million or confuse thousand and million. Practise with 3,050,008 as well: three million, fifty thousand and eight.

teach.heading: Value of each digit
bullets: The 2 is worth 200,000 and the 8 is worth 80,000.
The 4 is 4,000, the 5 is 500 and the 9 is 9.
teach.note: Ask: what is the value of the 0 in 7,284,509? Zero is worth nothing but holds the tens place. Compare with 7,284,590.

teach.heading: Up to ten million
teach.note: Link to real data: populations of cities and countries are given in millions. Ask pupils what is bigger, a city of 9,500,000 people or one of 950,000?

practice: What is the value of the 3 in 8,430,127?
Write 'two million, nine hundred and four thousand and sixty' as a number.
independent: Write as numbers: five million, three hundred and two thousand, one hundred; nine million and ninety-nine.
Make the largest and the smallest 7-digit numbers possible using the digits 3, 0, 8, 5, 2, 9, 1 once each. (No leading zero.)
exit: What is the value of the 4 in 2,846,513?
Write 'seven million and sixty-three thousand' as a number.
lessons.homework: Find three populations or distances above 1,000,000 in a book or online and write each in words and numerals.
lessons.send: SEND: place value chart, colour-coded groups of three digits. EAL: pre-teach million/thousand with the chart. Stretch: numbers to 1,000,000,000.

lessons.title: Comparing, ordering and counting in large steps
objectives: Compare and order numbers up to 10,000,000
Partition large numbers and count on or back in powers of 10

keywords.def: decide which of two numbers is bigger or smaller
split a number into parts by place value
the gap between two numbers or steps in a sequence

starter: Say Bismillah. Which is bigger: 5,430,000 or 5,043,000?

teach.heading: Compare from the left
bullets: First compare the number of digits.
Then compare digits from the left.
teach.note: Write the two numbers one above the other with commas aligned. Ask: where do they first differ? Use > and < symbols.

teach.heading: Ordering a list
bullets: Same millions; compare hundred thousands next.
teach.note: Model circling the digit being compared at each step. Pupils should read the finished list aloud to check it sounds right.

teach.heading: Partitioning
bullets: No ten thousands, so no ten-thousands part.
teach.note: Link back to Year 5. Ask for two different partitions of the same number to show flexibility.

teach.heading: Counting in steps
teach.note: Use a number line from 1,000,000 to 2,000,000. Ask: how many 250,000s make 1,000,000? (4). Crossing boundaries is a common error when counting back, such as 10,000 less than 3,005,000.

independent: Order from largest to smallest: 9,120,300; 9,102,300; 912,300; 9,210,030.
Partition 8,040,605 in two different ways.
Write a number that lies between 6,499,000 and 6,500,000 and has 7 as its tens digit.
lessons.homework: Find the populations of five countries or cities in millions (ask a parent or use a book) and order them from smallest to largest.
lessons.send: SEND: aligned place value chart, highlight the deciding digit. EAL: sentence stem 'is greater than because'. Stretch: negative multiples of large numbers, or numbers to 100,000,000.

lessons.title: Rounding any whole number
objectives: Round any whole number up to 10,000,000 to a required degree of accuracy
Choose a suitable degree of rounding in context

keywords.def: how close a rounded number must be, such as nearest 100
increase the rounding digit by 1 and replace later digits with zeros
keep the rounding digit and replace later digits with zeros

starter: Say Bismillah. Round 4,862 to the nearest 100.

teach.heading: The rule again
bullets: Look at the digit to its right.
5 or more, round up. 4 or less, stay.
teach.note: Underline the rounding digit and circle the deciding digit on every example. Replace all digits to the right with zeros.

teach.heading: Round 4,867,539
teach.note: Also nearest 1,000,000: hundred thousands digit is 8, so round up to 5,000,000. Check 4,868,000: hundreds digit 5, round up. Ask pupils what stays the same when rounding down.

teach.heading: When 9s carry
bullets: The 9s become 0s and carry to the left.
Always check with a number line.
teach.note: 9,996,400: ten thousands digit is 9, thousands digit 6, round up: 10,000,000. This produces an extra digit, a surprise for many pupils.

teach.heading: Choosing the accuracy
bullets: A city of 2,486,317 people is about 2,500,000.
Do not round money in the bank.
teach.note: Discuss when rounding is helpful (news, populations, estimating) and when exact numbers matter (pay, a bank balance, zakat calculations).

practice: A crowd was 54,382. Round it to a suitable degree of accuracy and say why.
independent: Round 9,999,500 to the nearest 1,000 and 1,000,000.
Round these to the nearest 10,000: 458,300; 1,235,000; 99,995.
A number rounds to 5,000,000 to the nearest million. Write the smallest and largest whole numbers it could be.
lessons.homework: Find five big numbers in the news or a book and round each one to the nearest 100,000 and to the nearest million.
lessons.send: SEND: number line with halfway marker, circle and underline prompts. EAL: model 'to the nearest...'. Stretch: smallest and largest numbers that round to a given value.

lessons.title: Negative numbers and intervals across zero
objectives: Use negative numbers in context
Calculate intervals across zero

keywords.def: a number less than zero
the difference or distance between two values
lower than the zero point on a scale

starter: A temperature of -4 degrees rises by 6 degrees. What is it now?

teach.heading: Negative numbers in life
bullets: Lift buttons below ground floor are negative.
Money owed can be shown as negative.
teach.note: Ask pupils for their own examples. A good one: a bank balance of -£40 means £40 owed. Use a vertical number line.

teach.heading: Distance across zero
bullets: From -8 to 15: go up 8 to reach 0.
Add the distance on each side of zero.
teach.note: Draw a number line and label the jump to zero. Many pupils subtract 15 - 8 = 7; ask why that is wrong. If both numbers are on the same side, subtract.

teach.heading: Falling temperatures
teach.note: Check by counting back: 6 - 15 = -9. Introduce counting on and counting back through zero.

teach.heading: Find the missing number
teach.note: Use a number line again. Missing number questions are common in SATs. A diver example works well: a diver at -35 m rises to -12 m, so the rise is 23 m.

practice: Find the difference between -7 degrees and 12 degrees.
A submarine at -45 m rises 28 m. What is its new position?
independent: Write the temperature difference: -3 to 9; -14 to -5; 8 to -6.
The temperature at night is -6 degrees and in the day is 11 degrees. How much does it rise?
A lift starts at floor -3 and goes up 9 floors, then down 5. Where does it stop?
Find the missing numbers: -8 + ? = 7; ? - 6 = -2; 3 - ? = -4.
exit: What is the difference between -5 and 9?
The temperature falls from 3 degrees to -7 degrees. By how much did it fall?
lessons.homework: Find temperatures for a very cold place and a hot place from a weather page or atlas and work out the difference.
lessons.send: SEND: vertical number line / thermometer; jump to zero first. EAL: pre-teach rise/fall/difference. Stretch: intervals with decimals such as -2.5 to 4.75.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting large numbers
objectives: Add and subtract numbers with up to 7 digits using written methods
Choose appropriate methods and check by estimating

keywords.def: writing numbers one above the other with place values lined up
swap 1 of one place for 10 of the place to its right
an approximate answer found by rounding

teach.heading: Column addition, 7 digits
teach.note: Continue: thousands 8 + 9 = 17, write 7 carry 1; ten thousands 6 + 7 + 1 = 14, write 4 carry 1; hundred thousands 4 + 5 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1; millions 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Answer 4,047,773. Estimate: 2,500,000 + 1,600,000 = 4,100,000.

teach.heading: Column subtraction
teach.note: Work through the exchanges one place at a time, starting from the first non-zero digit to the left of each zero. Check using the inverse: 3,182,526 + 2,847,689 = 6,030,215.

teach.heading: Estimate to check
teach.note: Ask: would 40,477,730 pass the estimate check? Using rounding spots place value errors quickly.

teach.heading: Choose the method
bullets: Use mental methods when numbers are friendly.
Use columns for large messy numbers.
teach.note: Show 5,000,000 - 1 = 4,999,999 mentally. Ask pupils to decide, calculation by calculation, which method is quickest and safest.

independent: A city had 3,482,600 people in 2010 and 4,157,900 in 2020. How many more people lived there in 2020?
Use the inverse operation to check that 6,403,200 - 2,555,900 = 3,847,300.
A charity collected £1,250,000 in year 1, £980,500 in year 2 and £1,375,250 in year 3. How much altogether?
lessons.homework: Write four large addition and subtraction calculations about populations, check each with an estimate and the inverse.
lessons.send: SEND: place value columns, digit cards, coloured exchanges. EAL: model 'carry' and 'exchange'. Stretch: calculations with decimals or three numbers.

lessons.title: Long multiplication
objectives: Multiply a 4-digit number by a 2-digit number using long multiplication
Estimate before calculating

keywords.def: a written method that multiplies by each digit of the second number
the answer to a multiplication
a zero written when multiplying by tens

teach.heading: Split the multiplier
bullets: Multiply by the ones digit first.
Then multiply by the tens digit.
teach.note: Set out the calculation in columns, with a clear line. Ask: why is the second line worth 20, not 2?

teach.heading: 3,426 x 24
bullets: 3,426 x 20 = 68,520 (put a 0 in the ones place).
teach.note: Check with an estimate: 3,400 x 25 = 85,000, which is close to 82,224. The placeholder zero is the key point.

teach.heading: 2,184 x 36
teach.note: Check with a different method: 2,000 x 36 = 72,000 and 184 x 36 = 6,624, so 78,624. Pupils can also use the area (grid) model.

teach.heading: Common errors
teach.note: Use squared paper. Ask: if 1,325 x 40 = 5,300 is wrong, how do you know? (estimate 1,000 x 40 = 40,000). Correct: 53,000.

practice: A box holds 48 dates. How many dates are in 125 boxes?
independent: A school buys 36 packs of 1,250 sheets of paper. How many sheets in total?
A coach holds 52 pupils. How many pupils can 27 coaches carry?
Find the error: 4,217 x 32 = 12,651 + 8,434 = 21,085. Correct it.
lessons.homework: Practise long multiplication on four calculations of your choice, each time estimating first.
lessons.send: SEND: squared paper, grid method alongside long multiplication. EAL: label each row 'x 4' and 'x 20'. Stretch: multiply 3-digit by 3-digit numbers.

lessons.title: Short division
objectives: Divide up to a 4-digit number by a 1-digit number using short division
Interpret remainders

keywords.def: the number you divide by
the number being divided
the answer to a division
the amount left over after dividing

starter: Write the multiples of 7 up to 70.

teach.heading: The bus stop method
bullets: Divide each digit in turn, from the left.
Write the answer above the line.
Carry the remainder to the next digit.
teach.note: Draw the bus stop shape on the board. Remind pupils to use known times tables. Ask: why do we start at the left?
Check with the inverse: 1,358 x 4 = 5,432. Show how the remainder becomes the tens digit of the next number.

teach.heading: Remainders
teach.note: Work 4,615 ÷ 6: 46 ÷ 6 = 7 r 4; 41 ÷ 6 = 6 r 5; 55 ÷ 6 = 9 r 1. The remainder after the last digit is the remainder of the answer.

teach.heading: Zeros and small digits
bullets: When a digit is smaller than the divisor, write 0.
teach.note: Example with a zero: 2,412 ÷ 4 = 603. Pupils often leave out the 0 and write 63.

practice: Work out 3,509 ÷ 7 and write the remainder.
independent: Calculate with remainders: 4,367 ÷ 5; 6,001 ÷ 9; 2,845 ÷ 7.
1,840 sweets are shared equally between 8 classes. How many does each class get?
Check using multiplication: 7,284 ÷ 6 = 1,214.
exit: Work out 5,234 ÷ 4 and give the remainder.
lessons.homework: Make up four short division questions with a 4-digit number and a 1-digit divisor and solve them with checks.
lessons.send: SEND: times tables grid, partially completed bus stops. EAL: pre-teach divide/divisor/remainder. Stretch: divide larger numbers by 11 or 12 using short division.

lessons.title: Long division
objectives: Divide up to a 4-digit number by a 2-digit number using long division
Check answers using multiplication

keywords.def: a written method used to divide by a number with two or more digits
a table of multiples of the divisor used to help divide

starter: Write the first ten multiples of 12.

teach.heading: List the multiples first
bullets: Use the list to find how many times 12 fits.
teach.note: Pupils write the first ten multiples of the divisor in the margin. This avoids guessing. Build the list by repeated addition and check 10 x 12 = 120.
Steps are divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. Check: 364 x 12 = 3,640 + 728 = 4,368. Say the four steps in a chant if useful.

teach.heading: A zero in the answer
teach.note: Check: 410 x 21 = 8,610; plus 3 = 8,613. Stress that the 0 is written in the answer, never skipped.

teach.heading: Another method: chunking
teach.note: Chunk: 15 x 300 = 4,500, remaining 1,485; 15 x 90 = 1,350, remaining 135; 15 x 9 = 135. Total 300 + 90 + 9 = 399. Show that either method is acceptable.

independent: A school hall has 975 chairs set in rows of 25. How many rows?
Calculate with remainders: 5,000 ÷ 12; 8,000 ÷ 15; 1,234 ÷ 21.
Check using multiplication that 9,072 ÷ 18 = 504.
lessons.homework: Solve four long division questions by listing the multiples of the divisor first, then check each with multiplication.
lessons.send: SEND: multiples table to fill in, grid paper. EAL: step prompts (divide, multiply, subtract, bring down). Stretch: divide by 3-digit numbers.

lessons.title: Interpreting remainders
objectives: Express remainders as fractions, decimals or by rounding
Choose how to deal with a remainder in context

keywords.def: the amount left over after dividing exactly as far as possible
go to the next whole number
ignore the remainder and keep the whole number

starter: Say Bismillah. Work out 59 ÷ 4 with a remainder.

teach.heading: A remainder as a fraction
bullets: The remainder is 3 out of 4, so 14 3/4.
teach.note: The remainder becomes the numerator and the divisor becomes the denominator. Check that 0.75 = 3/4.

teach.heading: Share £75 between 6
teach.note: Continue the division with a decimal point: 75.0 ÷ 6 = 12.5. Link to money: always give two decimal places. £250 shared equally between 8 families gives £31.25 each.

teach.heading: Round up
bullets: 9 buses leave 6 behind, so we need 10 buses.
teach.note: Ask: would you really leave 6 pupils behind? Context decides. Rounding up is needed when everyone must be included.

teach.heading: Round down
bullets: Cakes are sold in boxes of 12. We have 90 cakes.
teach.note: Rounding down is needed when only complete groups count. Discuss: the 6 leftover cakes could be sold separately, but they do not fill a box.

practice: Write 47 ÷ 5 with the remainder as a fraction and as a decimal.
Eggs come in boxes of 6. How many boxes are needed for 100 eggs?
£90 is shared equally between 8 people. How much does each get?
independent: Give the answer as a mixed number and decimal: 26 ÷ 4; 41 ÷ 8; 99 ÷ 5.
A teacher needs 1 chair for each of 135 pupils. Chairs are stacked in 8s. How many stacks are needed?
£250 of sadaqah is shared equally between 8 families. How much does each receive?
For each, write whether to round up or down: seats on a bus for 74 people (bus holds 20); posters made from 74 m of paper (each uses 20 m).
exit: Write 38 ÷ 5 as a mixed number and decimal.
Buses hold 30 people. 100 people need transport. How many buses?
lessons.homework: Write three word problems whose answers need a remainder to be rounded up, rounded down or written as a fraction.
lessons.send: SEND: bar models and worked examples. EAL: pre-teach remainder/share/equally. Stretch: remainders in division by 2-digit numbers.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Order of operations, factors and problem solving
lessons.title: Order of operations
objectives: Use the order of operations to carry out calculations with the four operations
Use brackets and squares correctly

keywords.def: the rules for which part of a calculation is done first
Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction
symbols ( ) showing what to work out first

teach.heading: Why we need rules
bullets: Everyone must agree on one answer.
teach.note: Ask half the class to work left to right and half to follow the rule. Compare answers. A calculator on scientific mode follows the rules.

teach.heading: BIDMAS
bullets: Division and multiplication, then addition and subtraction.
teach.note: Division and multiplication have equal priority, work left to right. Addition and subtraction likewise. Pupils think multiplication always goes before division.

teach.heading: Examples
teach.note: Write each stage on a new line. Show that brackets can change the answer. 18 + 6 x 2 - 4 = 18 + 12 - 4 = 26.

teach.heading: Same priority: left to right
teach.note: Work left to right when operations have equal priority. In the last example the bracket is done first: 8 - 3 = 5.

independent: Put brackets in to make true: 3 + 4 x 5 = 35; 20 - 8 ÷ 2 = 6.
Use each of 2, 3, 4 and 5 once, with any operations, to make 26.
lessons.homework: Write six calculations that need BIDMAS, solve them, then check using a scientific calculator.
lessons.send: SEND: BIDMAS reference card with colour-coded steps. EAL: pre-teach brackets/indices. Stretch: calculations with fractions or negative numbers.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Order of operations, factors and problem solving
lessons.title: Common factors, multiples and primes
objectives: Find common factors and common multiples of two numbers
Use common factors to simplify fractions

keywords.def: a number that is a factor of two or more numbers
the largest common factor of two numbers
the smallest common multiple of two numbers
a number with exactly two factors

starter: Say Bismillah. List the factors of 18.

teach.heading: Common factors and the HCF
teach.note: List factors in pairs and circle the matches. The highest common factor is the largest number in both lists.

teach.heading: Common multiples and the LCM
bullets: The lowest common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24.
teach.note: Context: one light flashes every 6 seconds and another every 8 seconds. They flash together after 24 seconds.

teach.heading: Simplify with the HCF
bullets: Divide top and bottom by the HCF, 6.
teach.note: Check that 3 and 5 share no common factors other than 1: the fraction is in its simplest form. Pupils can also divide by smaller common factors in stages.

teach.heading: Primes to 100
bullets: Is 97 prime? Not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7, so yes.

independent: Find the HCF of: 12 and 20; 28 and 42; 45 and 60.
Find the LCM of: 3 and 7; 6 and 15; 9 and 12.
Buses to the masjid leave every 15 minutes and every 20 minutes. They leave together at 4:00 pm. When do they next leave together?
lessons.homework: Choose three pairs of numbers below 50. Find the HCF and LCM of each pair and show your working.
lessons.send: SEND: factor pair templates, multiplication grid. EAL: pre-teach common/highest/lowest. Stretch: HCF and LCM of three numbers.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Order of operations, factors and problem solving
lessons.title: Multi-step problem solving
objectives: Solve multi-step problems using all four operations
Choose and check methods in context

keywords.def: a problem that needs more than one calculation
a diagram using bars to show the parts and whole of a problem
the opposite operation used to check

teach.heading: Four steps
bullets: Plan: which operations, in what order?
teach.note: Display the four steps. Ask pupils to underline the question and circle the numbers. Remind them to write units in the answer.

teach.heading: A building fund
bullets: Group A gave £25,350, group B gave £31,275.

teach.heading: Boxes and sharing
teach.note: Check: 72 x 12 = 864. Ask pupils whether the answer is reasonable: 12 families, 72 each, about 800 altogether.

teach.heading: Coaches and empty seats
teach.note: Start from the question 'how many seats are empty?' and work backwards to what you need to find first. Compare with a different problem where the 15 is given.

practice: A school buys 45 packs of 120 pencils and gives out 3,850. How many are left?
A mosque collects £4,500 on Friday and £3,750 on Saturday. This is shared equally among 5 projects. How much per project?
A train carries 1,248 passengers in 8 carriages. Each carriage has an equal number. How many in 3 carriages?
independent: A baker makes 24 trays of 36 buns. She sells 700. How many buns are left?
A fundraiser aims for £120,000. Week 1: £48,750. Week 2: £35,600. How much more is needed?
A coach trip costs £1,260 in total. 28 pupils share the cost equally. How much per pupil?
Write your own two-step problem using 18, 45 and 12 and solve it, showing a check.
exit: There are 36 boxes with 24 pencils in each. 150 pencils are used. How many are left?
£3,600 is shared equally between 15 people. How much each?
lessons.homework: Write and solve two multi-step problems about a trip or a charity event, using at least three different operations.
lessons.send: SEND: bar model templates and step prompts. EAL: highlight key words (altogether, shared, left). Stretch: problems with decimals or fractions.
